title: Explain the ACID properties (Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability) and transaction isolation levels.
shortTitle: ACID Properties and Transaction Isolation Levels

s1_definition.profdef: ACID describes the guarantees of a reliable database transaction. Atomicity means all statements in a transaction succeed together or none do (all-or-nothing). Consistency means a transaction moves the database from one valid state to another, never violating constraints. Isolation means concurrent transactions do not interfere with each other as if they ran one at a time. Durability means once a transaction commits, its effects survive crashes. Isolation levels (Read Uncommitted, Read Committed, Repeatable Read, Serializable) tune how much concurrent transactions can see of each other, trading strictness against performance.
s1_definition.analogy: When Rajesh transfers money to Priya at the National Bank of India, the debit from Rajesh and the credit to Priya must both happen or neither — never only the debit (that is Atomicity). The books must always balance and no rule is broken (Consistency). If two transfers run at once, neither should see the other's half-finished work (Isolation). And once the receipt prints "done," a power cut must not undo it (Durability). Isolation levels are how strictly the bank forbids one teller from peeking at another's unfinished paperwork.
s1_definition.oneliner: Atomicity is all-or-nothing, Consistency keeps rules valid, Isolation keeps concurrent transactions from interfering, Durability survives crashes — and isolation levels tune the Isolation strictness.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** ACID describes the guarantees of a reliable database transaction. Atomicity means all statements in a transaction succeed together or none do (all-or-nothing). Consistency means a transaction moves the database from one valid state to another, never violating constraints. Isolation means concurrent transactions do not interfere with each other as if they ran one at a time. Durability means once a transaction commits, its effects survive crashes. Isolation levels (Read Uncommitted, Read Committed, Repeatable Read, Serializable) tune how much concurrent transactions can see of each other, trading strictness against performance.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** When Rajesh transfers money to Priya at the National Bank of India, the debit from Rajesh and the credit to Priya must both happen or neither — never only the debit (that is Atomicity). The books must always balance and no rule is broken (Consistency). If two transfers run at once, neither should see the other's half-finished work (Isolation). And once the receipt prints "done," a power cut must not undo it (Durability). Isolation levels are how strictly the bank forbids one teller from peeking at another's unfinished paperwork.

**One line to remember:** Atomicity is all-or-nothing, Consistency keeps rules valid, Isolation keeps concurrent transactions from interfering, Durability survives crashes — and isolation levels tune the Isolation strictness.

sections.s2_technical:
Atomicity means a transaction is an indivisible unit. The database either applies every change (commit) or, if anything fails, reverts every change (rollback) so the database looks as if the transaction never ran. This is implemented with an undo log or rollback segment. For a transfer, if the credit fails after the debit, atomicity rolls back the debit so money is never lost.

Consistency means every committed transaction leaves the database satisfying all defined rules — constraints, foreign keys, checks, triggers. If a transaction would violate a rule (a balance check, a unique key), the transaction is rejected and rolled back. Consistency in ACID is about integrity constraints, which is subtly different from the "C" in CAP (which is about all nodes agreeing).

Isolation means concurrent transactions produce a result as if they had run in some serial order, so one transaction's intermediate state is not visible to another in ways that corrupt results. Perfect isolation is expensive, so databases offer tunable isolation levels defined by which concurrency anomalies they prevent. The classic anomalies are: a dirty read (reading another transaction's uncommitted change), a non-repeatable read (re-reading a row and getting a different committed value because another transaction changed it), and a phantom read (re-running a range query and getting new rows another transaction inserted).

The four standard isolation levels, from weakest to strongest: Read Uncommitted allows dirty reads — you can see uncommitted data; rarely used. Read Committed prevents dirty reads (you only see committed data) but allows non-repeatable and phantom reads; this is the common default in PostgreSQL and Oracle. Repeatable Read prevents dirty and non-repeatable reads (rows you read stay stable for the transaction) but historically allowed phantoms; it is the default in MySQL InnoDB, which also blocks many phantoms via next-key locking. Serializable is the strictest — transactions behave as if executed one after another, preventing all three anomalies, at the cost of more locking or more serialization failures that force retries.

```sql
-- Set the level for a transaction (PostgreSQL syntax):
BEGIN;
SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL SERIALIZABLE;
-- ... statements ...
COMMIT;  -- may fail with a serialization error → application retries
```

Durability means once `COMMIT` returns, the changes are permanently recorded and survive a crash or power loss. Databases achieve this with a write-ahead log (WAL) flushed to durable storage before acknowledging the commit, and often with replication so a single disk failure does not lose data.

Senior nuances: higher isolation gives stronger correctness but lower concurrency and more lock contention or retry, so you pick the lowest level that still protects your invariant. Many systems use optimistic concurrency (version columns) or explicit `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` row locks at Read Committed instead of jumping to Serializable, because targeted locking on the critical rows is cheaper than globally serializing everything. For a money transfer you either run at a level that prevents lost updates or you lock the affected rows for the duration. Also, modern databases implement isolation with MVCC (multi-version concurrency control), giving each transaction a consistent snapshot so readers do not block writers. And a Serializable transaction can abort with a serialization failure even when it did nothing wrong, so application code must be prepared to retry.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem — National Bank of India processes a transfer from Rajesh (SAV2001) to Priya (CUR3001). Two problems occurred historically: once, a crash after the debit but before the credit left Rajesh short by the amount (an atomicity failure), and once, two concurrent transfers from the same account both read the old balance and both succeeded, overdrawing the account (a lost-update isolation failure at too weak a level). The fix wraps the transfer in a single atomic transaction and uses row locking so concurrent transfers serialize on the account.

Our mini-project models a `TransferService` performing an atomic, isolated transfer: both legs happen or neither (atomicity), the account is locked so concurrent transfers do not interleave (isolation), and a rollback on failure preserves balances. A `Demo` shows a successful transfer, a rolled-back transfer, and two concurrent transfers that serialize.

The code will contain: an `Account` with debit/credit, an `AccountRepository`, a `TransferService.transfer()` that locks both accounts, applies both legs, and rolls back on failure, and a `Demo`.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: Rajesh (SAV2001) 1000000, Priya (CUR3001) 250000. One transfer of 50000, then two concurrent transfers of 100000.

Step 1: The first transfer acquires locks on both accounts in a fixed order to avoid deadlock — this is Isolation via row locking, equivalent to `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`. No other transaction can touch these rows meanwhile.

Step 2: It debits Rajesh (leg 1) and credits Priya (leg 2). Both succeed, so it reaches the commit point. On a real database the write-ahead log is flushed before commit returns, giving Durability. Both legs are now permanent — this is Atomicity's happy path.

Step 3: If instead leg 2 had failed (say Priya's account was frozen), the catch block restores both balances — Atomicity's all-or-nothing rollback — so Rajesh is not left short. The non-negative check on debit enforces Consistency.

Step 4: The two concurrent 100000 transfers each acquire the same locks, so they serialize: one fully completes before the other starts its critical section. Neither reads a stale balance, so there is no lost update. Rajesh ends at 1000000 - 50000 - 100000 - 100000 = 750000 and Priya at 250000 + 50000 + 100000 + 100000 = 500000.

Step 5: The demo prints the final balances, which are exactly correct, demonstrating all four ACID guarantees working together.

```
Oct 25, 2026 17:01:00 INFO: Transfer 50000 SAV2001->CUR3001 ok. SAV2001=950000.00 CUR3001=300000.00
Oct 25, 2026 17:01:00 INFO: Transfer 100000 SAV2001->CUR3001 ok. SAV2001=850000.00 CUR3001=400000.00
Oct 25, 2026 17:01:00 INFO: Transfer 100000 SAV2001->CUR3001 ok. SAV2001=750000.00 CUR3001=500000.00
SAV2001 final: 750000.00
CUR3001 final: 500000.00
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
ACID is the set of guarantees a reliable transaction provides. Atomicity means all-or-nothing: every statement commits together or the whole transaction rolls back, implemented with an undo log, so a transfer never leaves money debited but not credited. Consistency means each committed transaction leaves the database satisfying all its constraints — checks, foreign keys, unique rules — and this is about integrity, subtly different from the consistency in CAP. Isolation means concurrent transactions behave as if they ran serially, so one transaction's half-finished work does not corrupt another's result. Durability means once commit returns, the changes survive a crash, achieved by flushing a write-ahead log before acknowledging the commit. Isolation levels tune how much concurrency anomaly is allowed: Read Uncommitted permits dirty reads, Read Committed stops dirty reads but allows non-repeatable and phantom reads and is the common default, Repeatable Read also stops non-repeatable reads, and Serializable prevents all anomalies by making transactions behave as if run one at a time, at the cost of more locking or retry.

In our National Bank of India transfer service we had two historical failures: a crash after the debit but before the credit that left an account short, which was an atomicity failure fixed by wrapping both legs in one transaction, and two concurrent transfers that both read the old balance and overdrew the account, which was a lost update at too weak a level fixed by locking the affected rows with SELECT FOR UPDATE so concurrent transfers serialize. The senior nuances I add are that I pick the lowest isolation level that still protects the invariant and prefer targeted row locking or optimistic version columns over globally serializing everything, that modern databases use MVCC so readers do not block writers, and that a Serializable transaction can abort with a serialization error even when it did nothing wrong, so the application must retry. The line I remember is: atomicity is all-or-nothing, consistency keeps the rules valid, isolation stops concurrent interference, durability survives crashes, and isolation levels trade strictness against concurrency.
